E0983.summary: The Logos: for Philo, the seal by which the world was framed and of which the soul is an impression; for Atwood (Appendix), each man's fundamental faith and the Crown.
E0983.body:
Quoting Philo, Atwood gives the Logos as that “by whom the world was framed”, “the seal after the impression of which everything is made” [II.1 ¶43]; accordingly “the soul of man is an impression of this seal of which the prototype and original characteristic is the everlasting Logos” [II.1 ¶43].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) Atwood speaks in her own voice of “his fundamental faith, which is his individual Logos” [APP ¶101]: each man's individual Logos is his fundamental faith, to be fermented until it transmutes his whole being. She also identifies it with the Crown: “The Crown, to use Behmen’s and de St Martin’s phrase, is the Logos.” [APP ¶104].

E0984.summary: Lord Bacon, cited repeatedly by Atwood: partly as a witness favourable to the philosophers' stone and the ancients' wisdom, partly criticized for mechanical methods and ignorance of the Great Art.
E0984.body:
Atwood uses Lord Bacon both as support and as a foil.

**Support.** He reportedly experimented toward the philosophers' stone and recognized its possibility in the *Advancement of Learning*, without condemning the tradition [I.1 ¶82]. From the same work she takes his advice to regard the early sages with more reverence [III.2 ¶33; III.2 n30]. His Fable of Proteus (*De Sapientia Veterum* / *Wisdom of the Ancient*) supports, via Democritus, the principle of torture and restoration — to “torture and vex it in order to its annihilation” [I.2 ¶23] — and is quoted again with endorsement: matter, forced to extremity, runs through all forms and restores itself; he “lays hold of and works upon matter in the extremest degrees” [III.3 ¶61; III.3 n44], which Atwood glosses as the last exigence of life.

**Criticism.** She faults him for proposing mechanical dissolution and for not knowing the Great Art or its subject [I.2 ¶24; I.2 n19]; his “particular digesters applied to the fire” (*Sylva Sylvarum*; *History of Rarity and Density*) would expel the very nature prized [I.2 ¶24; I.2 n20]. His supposition (*Instauration of the Sciences*) that the understanding is too polluted by the fall to reflect total reason raises a difficulty, since introspection would then be useless [II.2 ¶21; II.2 n17]. Finally she calls him leader of the 'exterminating chase' of experimental philosophy, yet notes he recommended the pursuit of Causes and inquiry after the ancients' hidden Wisdom, 'though he knew it not' [IV.4 ¶30].

E0985.summary: Lorenz Oken, praised in the Appendix for treating nature 'in that higher way' and for an apparent inspiration into the science of created nature.
E0985.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) Atwood praises Lorenz Oken (cited in a Ray Society edition, London, 1847) as dealing with nature 'in that higher way' and as best evolving Causal Truth into the outward forms of life [APP ¶31]. Elsewhere she says he appears to have had an inspiration into the science of created nature [APP ¶96].

E0986.summary: The generative, fallen life, whose desire, opened upward, yields the Key.
E0986.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood speaks of “the desire of the lower life, the generative, the fallen life” [APP ¶97]; this lower life is thus identified with the generative and the fallen life, and its desire, opened upward, is said to yield the Key.

E0987.summary: Lucerna Salis Phil., a verse treatise Atwood quotes on the one universal matter (the Sages' salt), the stone, and its dissolution without corrosive.
E0987.body:
Atwood quotes this treatise (also given as *Lucerna Solis*, with a note referring to 'Lucerna Salis, from the Latin verse') in support of several points:

- The one universal matter, called the Sages' salt: “A certain thing is found in the world” [I.2 ¶9; I.2 n10].
- The stone, its growth, the Red Lyon and red Sulfur: “It is a stone and no stone, In which the whole art consists;” [I.2 ¶30; I.2 n32].
- The Stone is to be dissolved after the mind of the wise, “Nullo corrosivo adhibito” [III.2 ¶63; III.2 n46] (ours: 'with no corrosive applied').

Elsewhere Arnold, Lully and Artephius are said to agree with its description of whitening [III.2 ¶5].

E0988.summary: One of the ordinary mesmeric phenomena, named alongside prevision and community of sense, will and thought.
E0988.body: Atwood lists lucidity among “The ordinary phenomena of lucidity, prevision, community of sense, will, and thought” [II.2 ¶6].

E0989.summary: Named in a companion inscription declaring that corpse and sepulcher, contained and container, are the same.
E0989.body: A companion inscription under the name Lucius Agatho Priscus is quoted to the effect that contained and container are one: “Both corpse and sepulcher the same!” [III.3 ¶66].

E0990.summary: Raymond Lully, a confessed adept Atwood cites very often and with approval on the subject, the agent, secrecy, the inner work and the need for divine revelation.
E0990.body:
Atwood treats Lully as a major authority and endorses his testimony throughout.

**Witness to the art.** His own declarations are evidence for the England story; his alchemical writings are obscure but numerous and favourable to the art [I.1 ¶47–48; I.1 ¶76]. In the *Ultimum Testamentum* he is a confessed adept of known Christian zeal, with the story of gold for Edward II: “Converti una vice in aurum 50 millia pondo argenti vivi, plumbi, et stannic.” [I.1 ¶39, ¶46; I.1 n55] (ours: 'I once converted into gold 50,000 pounds of quicksilver, lead and tin'). She calls his *Theoria et Practica* one that “appears to us one of the very best pieces of Alchemical philosophy extant” [I.1 n58]. Norton's verse names him among masters who wrote obscurely [I.1 ¶15]; Ripley's verse names him as an authority, as having determined the science true, and as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [I.2 ¶6; II.1 ¶13; III.1 ¶62], and as one who revered Geber [I.1 ¶32].

**The subject.** An apparent contradiction (*De Arte Magna*) is explained: he denies only to a false position of the art [I.2 ¶7; I.2 n8]. The subject is of another nature and needs human art — “Imo argentums vivum nostrum est aqua alterius naturae” [I.2 ¶18; I.2 n17] (ours: 'indeed our quicksilver is a water of another nature') — Hyle, a clear compounded water, a third thing (*tertium*) [I.2 ¶29, ¶31, ¶42]. He agrees concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]; a quoted adept identifies his Lunaria with the authors' mercury [III.2 ¶25]. In the Appendix (a later layer) he supports the claim that nature has no pure conceptive vehicle: “The pure matter of the philosophers is not to be found on earth” [APP ¶43].

**Method.** He teaches patient rational inquiry and intimates Reason as a ferment; the golden bough is read as the subtle intellect: “Intellectus naturam habens subtilem ad intelligendum res intelligibles” [III.1 ¶13, ¶21; III.1 n26; cf. II.3 ¶11] (ours: 'the intellect, having a subtle nature for understanding intelligible things'). He warns against too strong a fire: “Let the heavenly power or agent be such in the place of generation, or mutation” [III.1 ¶55]. The Mercury “comes not but by help of ingenuity, and the Manual operations of man” [IV.1 ¶5]. First principles appear as cloud-like monstrous spirits, which Atwood reads as known from inner self-inspection [II.3 ¶30]. He adds “a sufficiency of the Divine Favour, and books to open the understanding and give it zest for truth” to Arnold's requisites [III.4 ¶20]; after a tedious common process he performed the Solution in nine days by the secret from God, which only God can reveal [IV.1 ¶36, ¶39]. He also charged strict secrecy [I.3 n15].

E0992.summary: In Synesius, two lights made manifest, one fixed and one volatile; when the lower rises upon the upper an incomparable Luminary issues.
E0992.body: Quoting Synesius, Atwood records that “there are made manifest two luminaries, the one fixed, the other not” [III.3 ¶60]: one fixed (male, below), the other volatile (above, ever moving). When the lower rises upon the upper, “there then issues forth an incomparable Luminary” [III.3 ¶60].

E0993.summary: The agent that takes the principal part when Sol is eclipsed, like Isis in the Mysteries; Atwood says it means the first prepared Subject, the Adepts' secret interior Fire.
E0993.body:
Atwood writes that, “Sol being eclipsed, the Lunar Vulcan acts a principal part, as Isis in the Mysteries” [III.1 ¶63].

Later she says the Stone is “prepared by those who trace nature with the assistance of the Lunar Vulcan” and explains: by “the Lunar Vulcan, as we long ago suggested, is meant the first prepared Subject” [IV.1 ¶29] — also called Diana and the Adepts' secret interior Fire. As 'Lunar Caustic' it needs outward stimulus: “this same Lunar Caustic is brought into act by an exterior excitation” [IV.1 ¶29]. The identity with the first prepared Subject is stated by Atwood herself.

E0994.summary: Lully's term, identified by a quoted adept with the quicksilver that authors call mercury.
E0994.body: An ancient and much esteemed Adeptus (Grasseus, per n26), quoted by Atwood, holds “that quicksilver, which authors call mercury, to be the same with Lully’s Lunaria” [III.2 ¶25].

E0995.summary: What Hermes suffered and toiled to obtain; not otherwise explained in the text.
E0995.body: Atwood reports that “to obtain the blessed Lunary of Diana, he had suffered much, and toiled incessantly” [III.2 ¶64], of Hermes. The text does not explain the expression further.

E0996.summary: Purificatory rites of the Mysteries by which the soul is liberated into a divine condition.
E0996.body: Atwood writes that “by the lustrations in the Mysteries, as they describe, the soul becomes liberated and passes into a divine condition of being” [II.2 ¶9].

E0998.summary: An image thrown forth, passive and ephemeral, identified with the downward-born nature and with Eve brought forth by Adam.
E0998.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood describes an image thrown forth, macrocosmic, passive and ephemeral for want of consubstantiality; its perfect beauty attracts the soul and, united to it, brings the ideal forth as actual offspring. She identifies it: “The macrocosmic image of the microcosm is the downward-born nature” and “It is the Eve which Adam brought forth” [APP ¶18].

E0999.summary: An adept who failed for five years and received the key by revelation; also rebuked by Nature for seeking the Stone without dissolution.
E0999.body: Atwood cites Madathan (*Mus. Hermeticum*, Lumen de Lumine) as an example: after failing for five years, he says, “I was entrusted with the Key of Power, by a secret revelation from Almighty God” [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n41]. She also quotes Nature rebuking him for trying to make the Stone without dissolution: “Dost thou think, says she, to eat the oysters, crabs, shells and all?” [III.2 ¶61].

E1000.summary: A voice quoted from Agrippa supporting the view that reason needs divine illumination.
E1000.body: Atwood quotes from Agrippa's Third Book of Occult Philosophy: “All is one soul, says the Magian, but reason, unless it be illuminated, is not free from error” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n29], in support of reason's need for illumination.

E1001.summary: Magic: an imputation against Bacon, in Paracelsus a natural secret of separation, the 'service of the gods', and in one passage the inward union of the elements.
E1001.body:
The records show several uses:

- **As imputation (Atwood).** Against Bacon “the imputation of magic has seemed ridiculous” [I.1 ¶38]; Atwood suggests that reducing it to natural skill may be as wrong as the old superstition. The medieval adepts are called “Magians, who were drawn about the fire of nature” [I.1 ¶39]. Ashmole “exposes certain principles of magic” [I.1 ¶62], and of Agrippa: “there stood the magician at last” [I.1 ¶64].
- **Paracelsus (quoted).** A natural, not specially divine, secret giving entrance into nature: “if that magic then were natural, certainly it was most wonderful, very excellent for quickness of separation” [I.2 ¶25].
- **Plato; Psellus (quoted).** The magic of Zoroaster, whose use is to perfect the soul by the power of materials; the cited view “calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods” [II.1 ¶51].
- **Its end (voice unclear).** The elements, unless united through the first love, “will never inward and essentially unite; which is the end and perfection of magic” [III.1 ¶50]. Boehme's phrase “bruise that composed magical body” [III.1 ¶48] describes a body that, bruised, becomes 'magical and hungry after nature'.

E1002.summary: The key prepared by the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus to open the Hermetic garden, said to have been lost by the Masons.
E1002.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood speaks of a magic Key prepared by the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus “to open the door into the Hermetic garden” [APP ¶100], and says the Masons lost it.

E1003.summary: A region in which every desire becomes prolific and embodies itself by the ethereal conception.
E1003.body: Atwood writes that “every desire is, in the magic region, made prolific” [IV.4 ¶10], embodying itself by the ethereal conception.

E1004.summary: Something the Fiery Dragon carries in its belly, in a passage quoted from Eirenaeus; not explained.
E1004.body: Quoting the same author (Eirenaeus, per n37), Atwood mentions the Fiery Dragon “which bears in his belly the Magic Steel” [IV.1 ¶43]. The text gives no explanation.

E1005.summary: The pure earth found at one's own center that commences Regeneration; also the Matter as an earth containing the recreative fire, the Land of Havilah.
E1005.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood places the magical earth at one's own center, quoting “nascitur in aere terra magica; in aethere clarificatur” [APP ¶89] (ours: 'the magic earth is born in the air; in the ether it is clarified'). She explains that there “you find that which is in the air or the vegetable life, that pure earth which commences the Regeneration” [APP ¶89], in contrast with the mineral earth of the lower life.

Earlier she calls the Matter “the true magic earth wherein is the recreative fire” [III.2 ¶8] and identifies it with the 'Land of Havilah, where good gold is' [III.2 ¶8].

E1006.summary: The dissolution which, with human aid, enables the Spirit to leave its extraneous forms.
E1006.body: Atwood writes of the Spirit that “Without the magical solution and human aid to fortify” [III.2 ¶61] it cannot leave its extraneous forms.

E1007.summary: The accomplished work or mastery of the Hermetic art, its goal and product; Atwood calls it a fiery form of Light inspisate and a type of the Christian Creed.
E1007.body:
Magistery is the adepts' name for the whole work, its mastery and its product.

**Atwood.** Wisdom guards “her universal magistery from an incapable and dreaming world” [I.1 ¶33], and men were “unable to perfect the same magistery” through the philosophers' obscurity [I.1 ¶36]; the word also appears in Geber's title 'The Sum of the Perfect Magistery' [I.1 ¶33, ¶36]. It is reached by communion with the ruling Spirit of nature [I.3 n19]. Man's virtue within himself to prove the Universal Source “was the foundation of the whole Hermetic magistery”, and “without this knowledge no one can attain to the magistery” [II.1 ¶8] — the knowledge of the vessel. In it the luminaries pass “through many phases from imperfection to perfection in the true magistery” [II.2 ¶26]; only those with “this passport can attain to the Magistery of life” [III.1 ¶13]. She defines it: “Which magistery is a fiery form of Light inspisate” [IV.2 ¶37], made manifest by triple introversion and multiplication of the hypostatic unit. The Adepts claim “their magistery not only corresponds, but is in every deed a type, and promise, and foundation of our Christian Creed” [IV.3 ¶27].

**Quoted authorities.** Flamel: “Having this, I easily accomplished the magistery.” [I.1 ¶57]. Geber: “the completement of matters sought after in our magistery” [I.1 ¶76]. Synesius: the soul is “drawn by our magistery out of its mine” [III.1 ¶70; cf. I.2 ¶33]. Bloomfield: “Our magistery is Three, Two, and One --- The Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone.” [IV.2 ¶36]. Eudoxus: “the knowledge of our Magistery comes rather by the Inspiration of Heaven” [IV.3 ¶16]. An unattributed verse: “Material of our Magistry a substance insensible.” [III.1 ¶7].

E1008.summary: A name for the matter calcined by its proper fire, also called lead of the wise; sown in the Philosophic Earth it dies and corrupts.
E1008.body: Atwood says the matter calcined by its proper fire “is called magnesia and lead of the wise” [I.2 ¶40]. A quoted scholiast writes: “our Magnesia, continues he, being sown in the Philosophic Earth, dies and corrupts” [I.3 n21], to conceive itself anew. *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* says the old philosophers described its making at large while concealing how to order it afterwards: “To create Magnesia they made no care, In their Bookes largely to declare;” [III.1 ¶65].

E1009.summary: In Atwood's Appendix, a will as center of attraction (two magnets in man are two wills); in the Greene Lyon verse, the fair white part left in the midst.
E1009.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes that “self becomes the magnet” [APP ¶122] and that “There are two magnets in man, i.e., two wills contending for man” [APP ¶124].

In *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* (quoted), the Magnet is the white part left when the matter separates from its black, light 'vile Erth': “Your magnet in the midst wilbe, Of Collour faire and white trust me;” [III.1 ¶65]; it must show full white, and the ferment is put into it as one fourth part.

E1010.summary: Used in Atwood's phrase 'the chain of the magnetic series', which moves when the Soul is drawn back into the Passive Spirit.
E1010.body: Atwood writes that when the Soul is drawn back into the Passive Spirit, “the first link in the chain of the magnetic series moves” [III.3 ¶10]. See also magnetic chain.

E1011.summary: The continuum from infinite pure light above all intelligence down to the darkness of Matter; the ladder of Celsus and Zoroaster.
E1011.body: Atwood describes Matter as lying at “the opposite extreme of the magnetic chain, which is extended a non gradu ad non gradum” [III.2 ¶54] (ours: 'from no degree to no degree'), from infinite pure light above all intelligence down to darkness. She identifies it: “this is that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54].

E1012.summary: Apparently the drawing power by which the gold attracts divine increase; the Stone is likened to an armed magnet.
E1012.body: The voice is unclear in the record. The Stone is likened to “an armed magnet included and circulating in a perpetual heaven” [II.1 ¶25]; the context suggests magnetical virtue is the gold's drawing power by which it attracts divine increase.

E1013.summary: The prophet whose Elijah prophecy frames Atwood's discussion of Elias the artist.
E1013.body: Atwood quotes Malachi 4:5–6, “Behold I will send you Elijah, the prophet” [IV.2 ¶12; IV.2 n4], to frame Elias the artist. The Refiner's-Fire messenger passage (Malachi 3:1–4) closes the section without comment [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n9].

E1014.summary: Attribution attached to The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, an allegorical verse account of the whole practice that Atwood gives 'by way of recreation'.
E1014.body: Atwood gives *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* 'by way of recreation' [III.1 ¶64] — 'in part', though the text is headed as unabridged — as an allegorical account of the whole practice: Green Lion, Sun and Moon, black/white/red, imbibition, ferment and multiplication [III.1 ¶65]. Its opening explains the name: “But our Lyon wanting maturity, Is called greene for unripenes trust me,” [III.1 ¶65]. She does not comment on it there. The attribution to Malden and the label 'Philalethean Lion Hunt' are uncertain from the records.
